title: We're Not Asking Permission to Refuse the Chromebook. We're Refusing It
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Cherkin argues that the real object of parental refusal is not the school-issued device but the internet connection that makes it work, and she documents what happens when a family tries to decline. Her framing point is that a Chromebook is a browser rather than a computer, so a district offering an internet opt-out while denying a device opt-out is offering a contradiction. She recounts her own experience in Seattle Public Schools, where an internet opt-out form dating to 2011 vanished from the website as soon as she submitted it, and notes a Pennsylvania lawsuit alleging a district repealed its own opt-out policy to block parents. The bulk of the piece is a case file: a Michigan parent's refusal letter, organized around nine concerns from efficacy and distraction to FERPA disclosure and surveillance software, followed by the district's refusal. Cherkin's annotation of the reply is the analytic move, since the district's own accommodation of paper alternatives for SchoolAI and paper M-STEP testing demonstrates that analog provision is possible where the district chooses. She closes by insisting on the grammatical distinction the title draws: a declaration of refusal is not a request for permission.
points: Locates the harm in internet connectivity rather than the hardware, and argues a downloaded curriculum or allow-listed tools would make the device a teachable object again.
Documents districts withdrawing their own opt-out mechanisms, including a 2011-era Seattle form that disappeared upon submission and a Pennsylvania policy repeal now under litigation.
Reprints a parent's nine-point refusal letter covering efficacy evidence, off-task time, persuasive design, FERPA disclosure, filter failure and generative AI.
Shows that the district granted paper M-STEP testing and concedes paper versions of SchoolAI work with no negative consequences, undercutting its claim that analog alternatives are impossible.
Notes that the district's answer relies on surveillance software, shifting the burden of managing device use back onto teachers.
quotes: A Chromebook is an internet browser, not a digital tool— if it cannot connect to the internet, it is virtually useless.
But as soon as I submitted the form, I was told by the district that “this option is no longer available” and the form disappeared from the website.

More recently, in a similar scenario, parents in Lower Merion County in Pennsylvania filed a lawsuit alleging that when parents attempted to decline student devices via a district policy that permitted device opt-outs, the District contrived to repeal and replace the policy to prevent parents from doing so.
Remove the ability for children to access the internet on school-issued devices and you return the computer as a tool that children do need to learn about in this highly digital world.

For parents interested in opting out of EdTech products and platforms or district-issued devices, it is helpful to see a great example of a parent declaring their intent to refuse (subtly different from asking permission to opt out).
The district says they “cannot approve the request” to opt out—it is not a request, it is a declaration;
I don’t know how a district can quite literally force a Chromebook on a child, but it appears they are willing to try.
Be persistent in your quest— do not accept “We cannot accommodate” as an ending; rather, it is an opening salvo.
